extracted.intended_audience: general educated readers of Montaigne; readers interested in moral/philosophical essays and practical judgment
extracted.subtask_description: Identify and list Montaigne's evaluative principles and practical criteria about judgment, authority, experience, speech, folly, and historiography as presented in the essay excerpt.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not overvalue dignities and offices
rubrics_metrics.description: Dignities and offices do not by themselves make a man superior; those to whom the king has given many offices may have no more in them than another who salutes him at a distance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observe behaviour and substance, not rank or outward ornaments. The crowd of adorers and ceremonial trappings often create undue credit; reassess persons according to their real merit rather than their place.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experience must be analysed and distilled
rubrics_metrics.description: The fruit of experience is worthless unless one knows how to extract from it something to form judgment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not accept mere tallies of events as proof of skill (e.g., a surgeon recounting cures). Experiences must be weighed, sorted and distilled to yield reasoned conclusions and increased skill.

rubrics_metrics.name: Silence confers an appearance of wisdom
rubrics_metrics.description: Silence is not only a countenance of respect and gravity, but very often of good advantage; a silent mien may procure credit of prudence and capacity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When uncertain or ignorant, preservation of silence can maintain reputation; speaking impertinently diminishes perceived stature (example: Megabyzus at Apelles's painting-room).

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not judge counsels solely by events
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘We are not to judge of counsels by events’ — success often disguises ill counsel, and fortune can justify foolish conduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the reasoning and process behind decisions, not merely whether they succeeded; historical examples (Carthaginians, Romans) show successful outcomes do not prove sound counsel.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognise the role of fortune in worldly affairs
rubrics_metrics.description: Most worldly affairs are performed by themselves; Fortune often governs results beyond man's prudence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain humility about human agency, especially in complex matters like war; avoid attributing disproportionate credit to human foresight when chance plays a large role.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid universal, sweeping judgments without justification
rubrics_metrics.description: Universal judgments (e.g., 'this is good, that is naught') signify nothing unless limited and explained; one must ask why or how it is so.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When confronted with general verdicts, require circumscription and reasons; insist on specificity and examples rather than broad assertions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Test whether a speaker truly understands borrowed material
rubrics_metrics.description: Most men are rich in borrowed sufficiency: a man may say a good thing or cite a sentence without seeing its force or origin.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When someone utters a striking phrase, inquire whence they have it and whether they comprehend it; do not grant credit merely for apt quotation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not publicly correct or rescue fools who show off knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: It is injustice and inhumanity to relieve and set right those who stand in no need of it; helping them often increases their arrogance and ineptitude.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Let them 'step deeper into the mire' so they may discern their own error; avoid doing 'initiatory and school instructions' in passing conversations with the unready.

rubrics_metrics.name: Folly is not cured by brief admonition; requires education
rubrics_metrics.description: Folly and absurdity are not to be cured by bare admonition; men do not become valiant or wise suddenly by one fine speech.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Correction is an apprenticeship that must be served by long and continued education; do not expect instant reform from brief rebukes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obstinacy and heated argument are signs of folly
rubrics_metrics.description: Obstinacy of opinion and heat in argument are the surest proofs of folly; arrogance and temerity fill the ignorant with assurance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beware those who show resolute disdain and assurance in debate; seriousness, gravity, and resoluteness alone do not equal wisdom (illustrated by likening such persons to an ass).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer study and deliberation to mere reading for certain works
rubrics_metrics.description: Some books are 'not a book to read, 'tis a book to study and learn' (e.g., Tacitus), requiring deeper engagement than casual perusal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge such works as study-material; expect sententious opinions and lessons for government rather than mere entertainment; approach with sustained attention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historians should report received beliefs without asserting them
rubrics_metrics.description: Give us history more as they receive it than as they believe it; historians relate common beliefs and popular rumours, not to regulate them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When reading history, distinguish between reported popular opinions and the historian's own endorsement; accept that chroniclers may record what was believed without affirming its truth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish author's own contribution from borrowed matter
rubrics_metrics.description: To judge a man's parts, one must know what is his own and what he has borrowed; the subject may make a man seem learned though parts are not original.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Attribute praise properly: evaluate invention, disposition, ornament, and language separately; be cautious in commending a passage until confirming originality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reputation often rises from place and ceremony rather than real worth
rubrics_metrics.description: An image of grandeur insensibly steals into opinion when a man is promoted; we judge by the prerogative of his place rather than by his worth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When someone rises and then falls, inquire why they were raised; treat sudden respect with skepticism and re-evaluate the person's actual capacities apart from rank.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid facile praise and superficial applause
rubrics_metrics.description: Cheap exclamations like 'That is fine' after a page of Virgil are a safe escape but signify lack of deep understanding; the cunning save themselves with such remarks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not let superficial admiration substitute for careful, line-by-line appraisal; cultivate the skill to identify where an author truly excels rather than relying on blanket praise.
